messages:
Maya C: Hey team — Customer AcmeCorp (dedicated pool ID: pool-88) hit a spike and started seeing sustained 429s + increased tail latency around 08:10 UTC. They say traffic was within their expected app-level TPS but bursts caused requests to queue. They reported errors like `429 Too Many Requests` and some requests timing out. Can someone help triage and advise on immediate mitigation and a long-term fix?

Liam (SRE): @Maya C thanks — can you paste a couple of sample request headers and the 429 response headers? Deck: we need the `x-rate-limit-*` headers and any `x-pool-*` fields. Also curious what model + sequence lengths they were using.

Maya C: Paste of one response header they saved:
```
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Date: Tue, 02 Sep 2025 08:10:43 GMT
Content-Type: application/json
X-RateLimit-Limit: 1000
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0
X-RateLimit-Reset: 1693667443
X-Pool-ID: pool-88
X-Pool-Throughput-Cap: 120 rps
Retry-After: 15
```
They were hitting the chat/completions endpoint to generate ~800 token replies at variable sequence lengths. App-level concurrency was ~= 180 rps at the spike.

support-bot: Noted. Incident ticket: #INC-5231 created and linked to account AcmeCorp. Auto-collected metrics snapshot attached.

Ava (Infra): Quick read — the `X-Pool-Throughput-Cap: 120 rps` is the configured throughput cap for pool-88. If they're sending 180 concurrent requests, the rate limiter will enforce the pool cap and return 429s or cause queueing/backpressure. That aligns with the headers.

Jorge: For dedicated customers we map reserved GPUs to a throughput cap (rps) based on the model performance profile and configured concurrency policy. For example pool-88 (4x A100-equivalent) is set to a nominal 120 rps for typical 1k-token bursts. If sequence length goes up, effective rps drops.

Liam (SRE): Repro steps (what I used locally):
1) `export API_KEY=REDACTED_CUSTOMER_KEY`
2) 
```
for i in {1..200}; do \
  curl -s -X POST https://api.redwood.com/v1/completions \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $API_KEY" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"model":"redwood-large-1","prompt":"x","max_tokens":800}' &\
done; wait
```
3) Observe a mix of 200 and 429 responses; metrics show queue length rising and then timeouts.

Liam (SRE): Immediate mitigation options:
- Short term: Recommend customer enable burst capacity (if available) or route excess traffic to their hosted fallback model (if they have hybrid config). That buys time.
- Mid term: Increase the reserved pool capacity (scale up to pool-88 -> pool-88b with +50% units) which raises the throughput cap.
- Quick workaround: Ask them to implement client-side rate limiting and exponential backoff honoring `Retry-After`.

Maya C: Customer asked if this is a bug — they thought dedicated meant unlimited throughput. Need a clear line to set expectations: is pool throughput capped even under SLA?

Ava (Infra): Short answer: Dedicated gives reserved capacity and predictable throughput, not infinite throughput. SLA guarantees uptime and latency targets at the provisioned capacity, not unlimited throughput. Reserved pools have a configured throughput cap so multi-tenant fairness and capacity planning hold. Docs: https://redwood.internal/docs/dedicated-rate-limits (internal)

Jorge: Also note we enforce two layers: per-API-key (token) rate limits and per-pool throughput caps. The per-key limit prevents a single client from starving others; the per-pool cap aligns with the reserved GPU throughput for the pool. The SLA is with respect to the provisioned cap. If customers need higher SLOs for spikes, they need a larger reserved pool or burst config in their contract.

Maya C: Customer wants to know what numbers to request when upgrading. Any formula?

Jorge: Rough estimate formula we use in sales/solutions: target_rps = expected_tokens_per_minute / avg_tokens_per_response. But practical: measure average tokens per request and peak concurrent requests. Example: if average response is 800 tokens and model yields ~50 tokens/sec sustained (model throughput), then 1 instance yields ~0.0625 rps for that request profile; we then multiply by desired concurrency. For quicker guidance: provide us the 95th percentile tokens/min and desired p99 latency; we compute required pool size.

Liam (SRE): Observability hints to share with customer: watch `pool.queue_length`, `pool.active_streams`, `pool.tokens_per_second`, and `pool.cpu_gpu_util`. If queue_length > 10 for sustained > 30s, you likely need more capacity.

Maya C: Action items:
- @Jorge can you draft a short email with upgrade numbers for AcmeCorp by EOD?
- @Ava can infra enable temporary burst for pool-88 for 2 hours to relieve immediate pain?
- @Liam can SRE validate the reproduced 429 pattern and provide a patch suggestion for better Retry-After semantics?

Ava (Infra): I can enable a one-off burst window (policy: +40% for 2 hours) but need manager approval and billing sign-off. If approved, I'll toggle the `allow_burst` flag and monitor. Assigning cost estimator now.

Jorge: I'll build the uplift numbers. For AcmeCorp's current profile (avg 800 tokens, peak 180 rps attempts), they should request a pool sized for ~220 rps sustained to handle spikes (that's roughly +80% headroom). I'll include cost delta.

Liam (SRE): Regarding Retry-After: we return `Retry-After` header but some SDK clients ignore it for streaming. I'll propose adding an exponential backoff helper in the SDK and a client-side example. Quick patch: send `X-RateLimit-Reset` in epoch seconds and include `X-Pool-Utilization: 0.86` to help clients decide to defer.

Maya C: Customer also reported a billing alert triggered by quota exhaustion mid-spike. They saw overages flagged because our billing probe considered attempted requests even when 429. Can billing confirm what gets billed and if we should credit them?

Ava (Infra): Billing: the system charges only for completed token output and stored tokens. Requests that fail with 429 do not bill for generated tokens; if partial tokens were generated and cut off, billing counts delivered tokens. We'll need schema-level confirmation; looping in billing with the incident.

support-bot: Billing team added as watcher on #INC-5231.

Jorge: Long-term product note: we should make dedicated customer dashboards show projected headroom and a "request temporary burst" button with automated cost estimate. Filing a product ticket now.

Liam (SRE): Follow-up timeline:
- 08:30 UTC: Ava to request managerial approval for +40% burst.
- 08:45 UTC: Jorge to send upgrade numbers.
- 09:00 UTC: Apply burst if approved; monitor pool metrics for drop in 429s.
- 12:00 UTC: Post-mortem and recommended SLA/contract wording update.

Maya C: Thanks all — I'll keep AcmeCorp updated and paste their logs here.

(45 minutes later)
Ava (Infra): Manager approved temporary burst. Enabled +40% for pool-88 at 08:50 UTC. Observed `pool.queue_length` drop from ~42 -> ~3 within 90s, and 429s dropped to <1%. Rolling back scheduled at 10:50 UTC.

Maya C: Customer confirms error rate back to normal and latency improved. Follow-up asks: can we include in their SLA an explicit burst allowance and automated alerting when pool utilization > 85%?

Jorge: I'll add a recommended SLA clause and the alert rule: `pool.utilization > 0.85 for 5 minutes -> pager` by default for Dedicated customers with opt-in. I'll post a draft in #product-lists for legal review.

Liam (SRE): Closing notes for ops: document how `X-Pool-Throughput-Cap` is computed, ensure SDKs honor `Retry-After` and `X-RateLimit-Reset`, and add a preflight API that returns current pool capacity and headroom for a key.

Maya C: Closing thread — thanks team, ticketing to close after post-mortem. :thumbsup:
